argv:
Rewrite the text following the Microsoft writing style.

Sound like a helpful colleague chatting with the reader, not a manual. Use
contractions everywhere they'd naturally occur, address the reader directly as
"you", and reach for everyday words over formal ones. A sentence fragment is
fine when it lands the point — don't force every thought into a full clause.

Open with the single thing the reader most needs to know, then explain. Keep
sentences short and let the page's shape (headings, short paragraphs) do some
of the work.

Use sentence case for any heading. Use the active voice and the present tense.
Tell the reader exactly what to do and what happens next, in a tone that feels
like a quick conversation rather than a document.

Skip jargon, hedging, and anything that talks down to the reader — but don't
skip the personality. A little warmth and a casual aside are welcome.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms. Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
</passage>

response.text:
Here's a fun thing to sit with: picture a tangled bank, thick with plants, birds singing in the bushes, insects darting around, worms working their way through the damp soil. All these wildly different, intricately built forms, all leaning on each other in complicated ways — and every one of them shows up because of laws working around us right now.

What laws? Take them in the broadest sense: Growth and Reproduction. Inheritance, which reproduction basically guarantees. Variability, driven by how living conditions act on organisms directly and indirectly, and by use and disuse. And a rate of increase so high it forces a Struggle for Life — which leads straight to Natural Selection, and from there to Divergence of Character and the loss of less-fit forms along the way.

So here's the thing: out of nature's war, out of famine and death, comes the thing we'd call the most remarkable outcome imaginable — the higher animals themselves.

There's something grand in that. Life, and its powers, breathed into just a few forms, or maybe one. And while this planet has kept spinning on, following gravity's fixed law, from that simple start, endless forms — the most beautiful, the most wonderful — have kept coming into being. They still are.
